facts.statement: The genus Beipiaopterus was named in 2003 by the paleontologist Lü Junchang.
facts.quote: The genus was named in 2003 by Lü Junchang.

facts.statement: The generic name combines the city of Beipiao in Liaoning Province with the Greek word for wing.
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from Beipiao City in Liaoning Province and a Latinized Greek pteron, "wing".

facts.statement: The only known species is based on a crushed partial skeleton of a subadult that lacks a skull.
facts.quote: The type and only species is based on holotype BPM 0002, a crushed partial skeleton of a subadult individual on a slab, missing the skull.

facts.statement: The fossil skeleton contains numerous vertebrae, a complete left wing, and both hind limbs.
facts.quote: It includes four cervical, fourteen dorsal, three sacral and nine caudal vertebrae, a complete left wing and two hind limbs.

facts.statement: Preserved soft tissues include wing membranes, a membrane on the tibia, a neck mane, and foot webbing.
facts.quote: Remains of the soft parts have been preserved, including partial wing membranes, a membrane attached to the tibia, a "mane" on the neck and webbing of the feet.

facts.statement: The animal had a wingspan of 1 meter and a body length of about 50 centimeters.
facts.quote: It had a wingspan of 1 m, and the animal itself had a length of about 50 cm

facts.statement: The fourth phalanx in the wing finger was naturally absent, a condition also seen in Nyctosaurus.
facts.quote: In the wing finger the fourth, normally most extreme, phalanx was absent; according to Lü this was not an artifact of preservation but the normal condition of the animal, one also known from Nyctosaurus.

facts.statement: A 2005 study revealed many blood vessels in the wing membrane, suggesting a role in thermoregulation.
facts.quote: In 2005 a study of the wing membrane by SEM (scanning electron microscope) was published, showing it had contained many blood vessels, which indicated a role in the thermoregulation.

facts.statement: Lü classified the animal in the family Ctenochasmatidae based on elongated neck vertebrae and humerus shape.
facts.quote: Lü assigned Beipiaopterus to the Ctenochasmatidae because of the elongation of the cervical vertebrae and the general form of the humerus.

facts.statement: A 2018 study placed the genus in a derived position within Ctenochasmatidae, contradicting earlier views of it being a basal member.
facts.quote: In 2018, Longrich, Martill and Andres recovered Beipiaopterus within the tribe Pterodaustrini, meaning that it was placed in a derived position within the Ctenochasmatidae, which contradicts its placement as a basal member.

facts.statement: This pterosaur lived during the Aptian stage of the Early Cretaceous in the Yixian Formation of China.
facts.quote: Beipiaopterus is a genus of ctenochasmatid pterosaur from the Early Cretaceous period (Aptian stage) of what is now the Yixian Formation of the China.

facts.statement: The animal lived between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago, spanning the Barremian to Aptian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Aptian (125.77 to 119.57 million years ago)
